query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase high-entropy alloys, exposure to service‐like cyclic stress combined with thermal aging induces localized solute segregation at the grain boundaries, leading to the formation of short‐range order that undermines grain boundary cohesion and fosters brittle behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy with a uniform distribution of alloying elements.
generation.intervention: Subject the HEA samples to thermal aging at elevated service temperatures in combination with cyclic mechanical loading.
generation.conditions: The alloy is operated under conditions typical of demanding engineering services, particularly where cyclic loading and elevated temperature stress are present; under low temperatures or static loads, the effect is expected to be minimal.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized grain boundary solute segregation resulting in the formation of short-range ordered regions.
generation.mechanism: The combined effects of thermal activation and repetitive mechanical stress enhance the mobility of specific alloying elements, causing them to segregate to grain boundaries. This segregation facilitates the development of short-range order that reduces local grain boundary cohesion, thereby promoting embrittlement despite the alloy’s overall single-phase nature.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated baselines, the thermally aged and cyclically loaded HEA will exhibit detectable nanoscale segregated zones (with short-range order) along grain boundaries along with a measurable reduction in impact toughness. In controlled comparisons with conventional alloys—where brittleness is predominantly associated with intergranular precipitation and not stress-driven local ordering—the mechanism will stand out as distinct.
generation.baseline: Untreated single-phase HEA specimens with a homogeneous distribution of solutes and established satisfactory toughness.
generation.boundary: The predicted embrittlement is expected to manifest only when the alloy is exposed to both elevated temperatures (sufficient for accelerated diffusion) and cyclic mechanical stresses. At temperatures below the activation threshold or under static loading conditions, the grain boundary segregation and resultant embrittlement should be minimal or absent.
generation.uncertainty: The specific alloying elements that most rapidly segregate, the kinetics of the short-range order formation, and the precise threshold conditions for embrittlement are not fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical single-phase HEA specimens. Expose one set to a combination of elevated temperature (mimicking service thermal aging) and cyclic mechanical loading, while maintaining the baseline specimens at room temperature and under static conditions. Utilize atom probe tomography and transmission electron microscopy to examine the grain boundaries for evidence of localized solute segregation and short-range order. Perform impact toughness tests and fracture surface analyses to correlate microstructural changes with mechanical behavior. For further contrast, test conventional alloy samples under the same conditions to validate the distinction between mechanisms.
measurements: Grain boundary composition and segregation patterns via atom probe tomography
Short-range order characterization via transmission electron microscopy
Impact toughness and fracture surface fracture analyses
Comparative mechanical property measurements between treated and baseline samples
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated HEA specimens do not exhibit any measurable grain boundary solute segregation or short-range order development, and if their toughness does not decline in comparison to the baseline (or is similar to that observed for conventional alloys under identical conditions), the hypothesis is falsified.
